articles.title: SV med 32 milliarder i økt skatt
articles.content:
Skattene økes med mer enn 32 milliarder kroner i helårseffekt i SVs alternative statsbudsjett.

I tillegg økes avgiftene med rundt 3,2 milliarder kroner i helårseffekt. Det er hovedsakelig klimaavgifter som økes. SV finner også rom til å fjerne dokumentavgiften for førstegangskjøpere av bolig.

Isolert for budsjettåret 2027 foreslår SV samlede skatte- og avgiftsøkninger på 25,6 milliarder.

Hovedforklaringen er en økning i formuesskatten på mer enn 16 milliarder kroner. Inntektsskatten økes med mer 3,2 milliarder, men SV sier to av tre vil få lavere skatt med deres opplegg.

– Skattenivået i dag er 24 milliarder kroner lavere i 2013 da Jens Stoltenberg sist var statsminister, sa finanspolitisk talsperson Marthe Hammer da hun la fram SV-budsjettet.

SV alternative budsjett legger opp til å bruke 309 millioner kroner mindre i oljepengebruk. En av satsingene er 10 milliarder kroner mer til kommunene, men bare 4 av milliardene gis som frie midler.

                        As well as tracking how many people move to Norway, the Directorate of Immigration (UDI) also monitors foreign nationals ordered to leave the country (with British citizens throwing up a surprise).

In 2025, Norwegian authorities issued formal deportation orders (utvisningsvedtak) to 5,002 foreign nationals, according to statistics from UDI.

A deportation order in Norway carries a formal entry ban, which prevents the person from returning to Norway for a certain period, or permanently in serious cases. It can even include a ban from entering the Schengen Area.

One of the main reasons a foreign resident can be deported from Norway is breaking the Immigration Act. This includes administrative violations like overstaying a visa, working without a valid permit, giving false information on residency applications, or not leaving the country after an asylum or visa refusal.

In 2025, 4,125 orders (which represents 82.5 percent of the total deportation orders) were issued on these grounds.

Foreign nationals can also be expelled from Norway after a criminal conviction, but this is much less common. Last year there were 368 such cases (7.4 percent of all deportation orders).

Contrary to popular belief, EU citizens are not exempt from being expelled from Norway, even though they have freedom of movement under the EEA Agreement.

In 2025, 500 orders (10 percent of all cases) were issued to European nationals. This can happen on grounds such as public order, public security, or abuse of rights.

In 2025, most deportation orders were given to nationals from South Asia and West Africa.

India had the highest number of cases with 949 in total. Of these, 941 were for immigration breaches and eight for criminal convictions. Pakistan was next with 918 orders, 917 for immigration breaches and one for a criminal conviction.

There was then a sharp drop. Bangladesh came third with 331 orders (329 for immigration breaches and two for criminal offences), and Nigeria in fourth place with 227 orders (218 for immigration breaches and nine for criminal convictions).

Combined, nationals from these four countries made up nearly 49 percent of all deportation orders in Norway in 2025.

Further down the overall list among non-EEA states were countries like Kenya with 112, Nepal (139), Ghana (111), China (78), the UK (62), Ukraine (59), and the United States with 42.

Australia and Canada recorded just 8 and 10 orders, respectively.

Among the European nationals, the highest number of expulsion orders was issued to citizens from Romania (160), Lithuania (89), Poland (75), and neighbouring Sweden (64), followed by the Netherlands (20), Latvia (13), and Spain (12).

UK nationals top list of convicted criminals deported

The figures show an unexpected trend in criminal deportations. Of the 62 British citizens ordered to leave in 2025, 35 were deported after criminal convictions. This made the UK the country with the most convicted criminals deported from Norway last year, ahead of Ukraine (33), China (31), and the United States (19).

A further 25 Britons were expelled for immigration status violations after losing EU freedom of movement post-Brexit.

READ ALSO: Indians, Brits and Syrians top Norway's permanent residency list

UDI statistics show a steady increase in expulsions in recent years.

Norwegian authorities recorded 1,210 deportation orders in 2021, 1,894 in 2022, 2,893 in 2023, and 3,302 in 2024. With the total passing the 5,000 mark in 2025, expulsion orders were more than four times higher than four years prior.

articles.content:

Photo by Billy Albert on Unsplash

                        One of the requirements to become a citizen in Norway is to pass either the social studies or the citizenship test. The Local has put together some advice on how to best prepare.

The process of acquiring Norwegian citizenship takes years, thanks to the residence requirements, and other conditions such as the language exams, background check, citizenship, or social studies test mean it's a far from straightforward road.

Still, it should be worth it in the end, even if you have to wait a lengthy time to receive a decision on your application due to long processing times.

The main difference between which test you may take will depend on the type of residence you were granted when you first moved to Norway.

The state offers an introduction to Norway programme to some people who move to Norway. This course, usually provided along with language training, aims to get new arrivals up to speed with the country.

Those typically offered these courses originally arrived in Norway on a family immigration or asylum seeker permit.

If you arrived in Norway under the EEA or work permit rules, then you will not have been offered this course.

For those who have done this introductory course, you will likely have been presented with the opportunity to sit the social studies exam. If you have sat and passed this exam in Norwegian, then you are all set, as the exam doesn't have an expiration date and can be submitted with the rest of your documents.

Even if you didn't get the chance to sit this exam in Norwegian or complete the course, fret not, the syllabus for the course will be the same as for the citizenship exam. Therefore, you should have picked up a few things that will be useful for the test.

Most applicants who didn't do the social studies course will probably prefer the citizenship test as it is slightly easier.

The reason it's easier isn't the content of the test itself, as both tests are drawn from the same syllabus. Instead, the language used in the citizenship test is considered more accessible.

Both tests require knowledge of Norwegian history, the school system, healthcare, politics, and geography. They also include questions on societal norms in Norway, working life, and government agencies.

The syllabus is available online and can be divided into the topics of "education skills and the labour market," "family, health and daily life," and "Norway now and before."

These different topics are broken down into various sub-topics. These topics will cover how a system works in Norway and the cultural values behind a particular system – understanding both will give you the tools you need to ace either exam.

Course materials are available in several languages (however, the online portal can be glitchy). The curriculum is found on the website of HK-dir (The Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills).

Thankfully, having the curriculum available should help.

Another helpful aspect of the online curriculum is that it includes discussion points and multiple-choice questions.

For the discussion points, ask somebody to read out the questions to you in English or Norwegian as another way of testing your retention.

There is also an official mock available online. The only downside is that the questions don't change. Still, it should be good for familiarising yourself with how your knowledge will be tested and learning the language used for the test.

There are also unofficial practise exams online. Some of these charge users for access to example questions. Still, there are free mocks available online that applicants can take.

With the right preparation, you should be able to sit the test when you feel ready rather than rushing into it. Local municipalities are responsible for providing the exams and there are quite a few opportunities to take the test throughout the year.

If you need more time to get up to speed with your Norwegian reading skills, or the syllabus then its better to wait a few weeks or couple of months for more slots to open up.

Alternatively, if you want everything ready to submit when you meet the residence requirements, and your Norwegian skills are good enough, then you can take the test ahead of time.

Either way, there's no point in booking a police appointment to hand your documents in until you've passed the test – so there shouldn't be any need to put yourself under any pressure.

                        Let's peek behind closed doors at Norwegian bedroom habits.

Given how many internationals move to Norway for love, understanding local intimacy habits can be a practical cultural survival skill, whether you are looking for fresh ideas or simply discovering a shocking reality.

Here are some findings from a survey conducted by YouGov for the adult boutique Nytelse.no that reveal eye-opening insights.

Only 54 percent of Norwegians kiss their partner on a daily basis.

This might come as a surprise to internationals from cultures where showing affection is more common.

If you feel your sex life has slowed down since moving to Norway, you are far from alone. About 59 percent of people have sex once a month or less, and only 36 percent do so weekly. Still, 74 percent wish they had sex at least once a week, and nearly a third want a higher sex drive.

                        PM Støre rejects 'us versus them' approach to immigration in Norway, health minister wants to shake up the healthcare system, getting ready for Halloween, and more news this Friday.

PM Støre rejects 'us versus them' approach to immigration in Norway

​Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre delivered an opening speech at the annual conference of the Directorate of Integration and Diversity (Integrerings- og mangfoldsdirektoratet, or IMDi) in Oslo, declaring that Norway’s growing diversity is now a key part of the country’s identity.

Støre talked about how Norway’s population has changed over the last sixty years, comparing the country he grew up in to today’s society:

"I was born in 1960. You can do the math yourselves, and in the census that year, there were 62,500 foreign-born people living in Norway. That was 1.7 percent of the population. Today, I am 66, and the total immigrant population is over 1.2 million—21.7 percent of the population.

"Out of these 1.2 million, 238,000 are Norwegian-born with an immigrant background, and 340,000 are individuals with a refugee background; that is, from 62,000 to 1.2 million. That is fundamental. And I think one of the most important things, is that this is Norway, and this is who we are. "

Støre emphasised that immigration should not be seen as a contest between the majority and minority groups, referencing King Harald V's iconic 2016  speech on inclusivity:

"The most important thing we must do in our minds is realise that this is not an exercise of 'us versus them'—between a majority population and a minority population—because we are our country. I think King Harald phrased it very well when he said that this is us in Norway, all of us together. We share these tasks together, and we face our challenges together."

You can watch the video of the speech on the website of the newspaper Nettavisen.

Norwegian vocabulary: minoritetsbefolkning - minority population

Date set for renewal of Norway's Norgespris electricity scheme for 2027

The government has announced that households in Norway will need to take action if they want to keep or join the government’s Norgespris electricity scheme next year, as current agreements expire on December 31st and do not renew automatically.

The government introduced the voluntary Norgespris scheme in October 2025 to help households and holiday home owners avoid big changes in electricity prices by offering a steady, subsidised  fixed rate.

To underline the scheme's impact, the government released figures showing in the third quarter (July to September), households saved almost 4.5 billion kroner compared to spot prices, whereas households relying solely on standard electricity subsidies saved under 0.8 billion kroner over the same period.

Analysing its first full year, Norgespris paid out nearly 19.8 billion kroner in support.

"The development of power prices in 2026 shows that Norgespris has been vital. It has given people more predictable electricity bills and security for their wallets," said Energy Minister Terje Aasland in a press statement.

Since the scheme began, the price has stayed at 40 øre per kilowatt-hour (without VAT), however in the 2027 national budget, the government wants to raise the fixed rate to 45 øre per kWh (without VAT). If parliament agrees, this would bring the price to around 56 øre per kWh including VAT starting from the first day of January.

If you want to join the Norgespris scheme next year, you can do so from Tuesday, January 5th, 2027.

Health minister wants the biggest hospital reform in 25 years

Health Minister Jan Christian Vestre has announced that he wants to “shake up” the healthcare system in Norway.

On Monday, an expert committee will deliver recommendations on reorganising hospital governance, which will help him draft a proposal for possible changes, as reported by newspaper Aftenposten.

The committee's goal has been to create a health service that is better connected between hospitals, the municipal health service, GPs, etc., while also considering how to manage the investments and budgets.

​"We have put off many challenges ahead of us for a little too long. Now we actually have to shake things up and think new and different," Vestre told news agency NTB. "I envision the biggest change in 25 years," he added, talking about the current health enterprise model introduced in the early 2000s.

​The current "health enterprise" model split specialist hospital care into four state-owned regional health authorities that are separate from direct political control. Critics say this model is too bureaucratic and puts up barriers between state hospitals and local care services. As a result, vulnerable people, like elderly patients or those with complex mental health and addiction needs, are often moved between disconnected systems.

The minister said he is concerned that patients are sent between different treatments, information is not shared correctly, and follow-ups are missed

He also explained the reform should help patients and front-line healthcare workers rather than administrative structures. The aim is to better connect hospital and local services, so patients get good care no matter who is in charge of it.

The ministry plans to send proposals to parliament and hopes to make the changes before Vestre's term ends in autumn 2029.

Halloween has grown significantly in popularity across Norway over recent decades, so you can expect plenty of people out celebrating across the country on Friday, October 30th and Saturday, October 31st.

In residential neighbourhoods, you’ll see children in costumes going door-to-door for trick-or-treating (knask eller knep in Norwegian), but plenty of adults will also be heading out to themed parties and nightlife events.

If you are making weekend plans, we have listed the best activities in Oslo, Bergen, Stavanger, Trondheim, and Tromsø. The best places to celebrate Halloween in Norway this year

Following the halloween celebrations, November 1st marks All Saints' Day (Allehelgensdag), which in contrast is traditionally a day of reflection in Norway, when people visit cemeteries to light candles on the graves of deceased loved ones.

Thanks to Norway's growing international community,  you will also see global traditions in major cities, like the Mexican Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) events with altars and cultural activities.
